title: Longevity as Its Own Form of Greatness
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Sparked by a James Clear newsletter observation that "longevity is its own form of greatness," Stuart applies the idea to teaching and complicates it. He affirms that staying in the profession for decades (naming real colleagues like Doug Stark, Diane Wanamaker, Jackie Berndt, and Tracy Franklin) is a form of greatness he'd choose over a short, dramatic career like Erin Gruwell's four years fictionalized in Freedom Writers. But he draws a sharper distinction between two ways of achieving that longevity: "Way One," merely doing your time and counting down to retirement, versus "Way Two," investing your heart and mind into students, colleagues, and community month after month. Only the second kind of longevity, he argues, earns the label of greatness - the first merely reaches the finish line. He closes by cautioning that even Way Two longevity requires moderation and attention to life beyond school, naming people outside the classroom who depend on a teacher in ways no student ever will.
points: Distinguishes two categories of career longevity - "doing your time" versus "investing your time" - arguing only the second genuinely earns the label of greatness.

Uses a real comparison (Erin Gruwell's dramatized four-year career in Freedom Writers versus named colleagues with full multi-decade careers) to argue sustained, unglamorous dedication outweighs short-term intensity.
Names longevity's necessary counterweight explicitly: moderation and an eye toward one's whole life, not just the job, since people outside school depend on the teacher too.
Credits and directly engages an outside source (James Clear) rather than presenting the idea as wholly original, modeling how to build on borrowed insight.
quotes: Business: Can you maintain cash flow and stay in business? Longevity is its own form of greatness.

Longevity in this profession is an exceptional kind of greatness. If you let me choose between one Erin Gruwell (whose four-year teaching career - yes, four years - was the highlight of the memoir and film Freedom Writers) and one Doug Stark or Diane Wanamaker or Jackie Berndt or Tracy Franklin
Way One: Do your time. Avoid getting fired. Deal with the kids you teach. Deal with their parents. Count each day as one day closer to retirement when you get to do what you want to do.
Way Two: Invest your time, month by month becoming better. Engage your heart and mind and strength in the kids that you teach, for the duration of each working hour.
Way One can get you to the finish line of a career, but it's surely not greatness. It's better than making your living selling cocaine, I guess. But not much of a life.

I can think of no career that will leave one as grateful for having had the chance to do the work, so long as you're able to conduct it with moderation, with an eye toward your whole life and not just your job.
